title: Efficacy and safety of once-weekly semaglutide 2.4 mg for weight management in participants from China: A prespecified analysis of the STEP 7 randomized clinical trial

what_it_measured.text: Abstract Aim: To evaluate the efficacy and safety of semaglutide 2.4 mg versus placebo for weight management in a population of Chinese adults with overweight or obesity.

endpoint.text: The primary endpoints were percentage change in body weight from baseline to Week 44 and the proportion of participants who achieved ≥5% reduction in body weight from baseline.

Additionally, the effect of semaglutide 2.4 mg versus placebo on body weight change from baseline was consistent across subgroups (Table S3). 3.3 | Confirmatory secondary endpoints The observed proportion of participants achieving a ≥10% or ≥15% change in body weight at Week 44 was greater with semaglutide 2.4 mg versus placebo, as odds favoured semaglutide 2.4 mg (Table 2; Figure 1B).

Baseline characteristics were balanced across treatment groups (Table 1). 3.2 | Primary endpoints The mean body weight change at Week 44 was 11.8% with semaglutide 2.4 mg versus 3.5% with placebo (estimated treatment difference [ETD] –8.3 percentage points; 95% CI –10.2, 6.4; p < 0.0001), for the treatment policy estimand (Figure 1A); results were consistent for the trial product estimand (Figure S4; Table S2).

reported_results.text: At Week 44, a greater proportion of participants treated with semaglutide 2.4 mg achieved ≥5% body weight loss versus placebo (85.4% vs. 26.8%): odds ratio 16.1; 95% CI 8.4, 30.9; p < 0.0001.

Estimated change in mean body weight from baseline to Week 44 was 11.8% with semaglutide 2.4 mg versus 3.5% with placebo (estimated treatment difference 8.3%; 95% confidence interval [CI] –10.2, 6.4; p < 0.0001).
The primary endpoints were percentage change in body weight from baseline to Week 44 and the proportion of participants who achieved ≥5% reduction in body weight from baseline.

Materials and Methods: In STEP 7 (NCT04251156), a double-blind, phase 3a trial, adults from a predominantly East Asian population with overweight or obesity, with or without type 2 diabetes, were randomized 2:1 to once-weekly subcutaneous semaglutide 2.4 mg or placebo for 44 weeks as an adjunct to a reduced-calorie diet and increased physical activity.
For the participants with T2D at screening, the observed mean changes in HbA1c from baseline to Week 44 were 2.0% for semaglutide 2.4 mg and 0.6% for placebo.
A greater proportion of participants who received semaglutide 2.4 mg decreased their OAD than those who received placebo (21.6% vs. 4.0%) (Table 2).
